title: Strings: immutability, == and equals()
body: Java Strings are immutable: methods such as toUpperCase() or concat() return a new String and leave the original unchanged. String literals are stored in the string pool, so identical literals share one pooled object. == compares references (whether two variables point to the same object), while equals() compares the characters. new String("x") always creates a separate object. For heavy concatenation inside loops use StringBuilder, which is mutable and avoids creating many temporary objects. Because Strings are immutable they are thread-safe and work well as HashMap keys.
interview_tip: Always compare String contents with equals() (or equalsIgnoreCase()); mention the string pool when asked why == sometimes appears to work.

title: Collections: List, Set and Map
body: The Collections Framework offers three main families. A List is ordered and allows duplicates: ArrayList gives fast random access, LinkedList gives cheap insertion and removal at the ends. A Set rejects duplicates: HashSet has no guaranteed order, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, TreeSet keeps elements sorted. A Map stores key-value pairs with unique keys: HashMap (no order, allows one null key), LinkedHashMap (insertion order) and TreeMap (sorted keys). List.of(), Set.of() and Map.of() create unmodifiable collections; calling add() on them throws UnsupportedOperationException.
interview_tip: A frequent question is ArrayList vs LinkedList: give the time complexity of get(i) (O(1) vs O(n)) and of adding or removing at the front.

title: Exceptions: checked, unchecked and finally
body: All exceptions extend Throwable. Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception but not of RuntimeException, such as IOException) must be caught or declared with throws, or the code will not compile. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses such as NullPointerException and ArithmeticException) usually signal programming bugs and need not be declared. Errors such as OutOfMemoryError are serious JVM problems. A finally block runs whether or not an exception occurs, which makes it the place for cleanup; try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources automatically. Order catch blocks from most specific to most general.
interview_tip: Know the difference between throw (raises an exception object) and throws (declares exceptions in a method signature).

title: Overloading, overriding and static members
body: Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in one class; the compiler picks one at compile time, preferring exact or widening matches, then boxing, then varargs. Overriding means a subclass redefines an inherited instance method with the same signature; the JVM chooses the version at run time from the object's actual class, which is runtime polymorphism. Static methods are not overridden, only hidden, and are chosen by the reference type. A static field has one copy shared by all objects, while each object gets its own copy of an instance field.
interview_tip: Use the @Override annotation in code you write in interviews; it makes the compiler catch signature mistakes.

title: equals() and hashCode() for HashMap keys
body: HashMap and HashSet first use hashCode() to choose a bucket and then equals() to find the matching key. The contract: objects that are equal according to equals() must return the same hashCode(). If you override equals() but not hashCode(), two logically equal objects can land in different buckets and lookups fail. Unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), which only slows lookups. Keys should be immutable, because changing a field used in hashCode() after insertion can make the entry unreachable. Java 17 records generate consistent equals() and hashCode() automatically.
interview_tip: When asked what happens if only equals() is overridden, explain that a HashSet may then store logically duplicate objects.
